title: US Proposes PERM Overhaul: 90-Day Job Ads and Layoff Bars for EB-2, EB-3 Sponsors
excerpt: The Labor Department's first major PERM rewrite in two decades would lengthen recruitment, end the Schedule A bypass and bar sponsors with recent layoffs. It is a proposal only — comments close January 19, 2027, and current rules still apply.
body:
• The US Department of Labor has proposed the first major overhaul of the PERM labour certification programme in about 20 years, published in the Federal Register on November 17, 2026. Nothing in current PERM rules changes yet — this is a proposal open for public comment until January 19, 2027.
  • Employers sponsoring EB-2 and EB-3 green cards would have to recruit US workers for at least 90 days, advertise the salary, and file the full supporting documents — including US applicants' resumes — with the application.
  • An employer that laid off US workers in the same or a similar occupation in the area within the previous two years would be barred from filing, replacing today's six-month notify-and-consider rule.
  • Schedule A would be eliminated, ending the labour-market-test bypass that nurses, physical therapists and people of exceptional ability in the sciences and arts currently use.

The US Department of Labor (DOL) has proposed a sweeping rewrite of the PERM permanent labour certification programme — the labour-market test most employers must pass before sponsoring a foreign employee for an EB-2 or EB-3 green card. The proposed rule, "Modernizing the Labor Market Test and Improving Protections for U.S. Workers in the PERM Immigrant Visa Program," was published in the Federal Register on November 17, 2026 (docket ETA-2026-0133). It is the first major revision of PERM in roughly two decades, and it is a proposal, not a change in force: the existing regulations remain in place while DOL takes public comment.

Who is affected — and who is not

The proposal touches employers and the workers they sponsor through PERM-based EB-2 and EB-3 cases — the route used by a large share of Indian professionals on H-1B visas who are waiting in the employment-based green card backlog, and by the technology companies, consulting and staffing firms, hospitals and universities that sponsor them. Counted here: the employer's recruitment and filing duties before an I-140 petition can follow. Not counted: H-1B status itself, the annual green card caps, and applications already filed — the proposal does not cancel existing green card applications or revoke work visas, and it sets no nationality-based restriction.

What would change

Longer, more uniform recruitment. The separate recruitment tracks for professional and non-professional occupations would be replaced by a single standard. Required advertising — including the state workforce agency job order — would have to run for no less than 90 calendar days, up from the current framework built around a 30-day job order, and would use the channels employers customarily use today: the employer's own website, at least one external job-search site, and social media where that is customary for comparable roles. The offered salary or wage range would have to appear in the advertisements. All recruitment would need to be completed between 30 and 60 days before filing, and the application filed within 30 days of recruitment ending.

Documents filed up front. Instead of producing evidence mainly when audited, employers would submit the supporting record with the application itself: the prevailing wage determination, the notice of filing, evidence of all recruitment, a detailed recruitment report, and the resumes and applications received from US workers.

A two-year layoff bar. The current rule — a six-month lookback under which an employer must notify and consider laid-off US workers — would become a categorical bar: a PERM application could not be approved if the employer had conducted relevant layoffs of US workers in the same or a similar occupation in the area of intended employment within the previous two years. Employers would also carry a continuing duty to report a qualifying layoff after filing, through I-140 adjudication, as the law firm Nixon Peabody notes in its analysis of the proposal.

Schedule A eliminated. DOL would stop administering Schedule A, the list of occupations — professional nurses, physical therapists, and individuals of exceptional ability in the sciences or arts — that are currently pre-certified as facing a shortage of US workers and so bypass the labour-market test. Those workers would not lose green card eligibility; their employers would have to run the full PERM process like everyone else.

Longer notice. The notice of filing would have to be posted at least 10 business days before filing and remain posted through approval of the I-140 petition.

What to do next

For now, nothing about a pending or planned case changes: current PERM rules still govern, and immigration lawyers advising employers are cautioning against re-engineering recruitment programmes around a rule that may be revised before it is finalised — and that, as Legal 500's summary notes, will likely face court challenges if adopted. Employers, industry groups and affected workers can file comments on the proposal through the Federal Register docket ETA-2026-0133 until January 19, 2027. After the comment period closes, DOL reviews the submissions and decides whether to issue a final rule; there is no fixed deadline for that decision. Under the proposal's own transition terms, a final rule would take effect 60 days after publication, with a further 30-day window in which filings could still be made under today's rules.
